analysis.one_liner: Caps prescription drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries at manufacturers' average foreign prices.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut seniors' drug prices to levels paid abroad drew 127 cosponsors, but it never got a vote in either committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any drug maker that sells drugs to the U.S. government to also sell to pharmacies, in amounts matched to what Medicare beneficiaries buy, at a price no higher than what the manufacturer charges on average in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. A manufacturer that refused could be barred from federal contracts. It also extended the same lower prices to drugs for Medicare patients in hospice care. The bill was sent to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans who at the time had no drug benefit and paid full retail prices. The bill's findings cite evidence that seniors often paid far more than buyers abroad and than the drug makers' favored U.S. customers like insurers and HMOs, and estimate the policy would cut brand-name drug prices for many seniors by about 40 percent on average.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying full retail drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Each manufacturer that contracts with the U.S. government would have to supply pharmacies, in quantities matching what Medicare beneficiaries buy, at a price no greater than the manufacturer's average foreign price across six covered nations.

The bill's findings state the policy would reduce prices for brand-name prescription drugs for many Medicare beneficiaries by an average of 40 percent, and that seniors often pay twice as much as consumers abroad and in some cases ten times more.

Drugs furnished to Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare-certified hospice programs would count toward the quantity pharmacies can buy at the capped price, extending the benefit to terminally ill patients.
The bill's findings argue that lower drug prices would improve seniors' health and lower Medicare costs to federal taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would have to give up the gap between what they charge in the U.S. market and their lower foreign prices. The bill's own findings note industry profits of $27.3 billion in 1999 sustained by pricing seniors paid more for. Any reduced revenue could, over time, affect research spending, though the bill does not address that tradeoff.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is debarment — barring a noncompliant manufacturer from all federal contracting and subcontracting. A large drug maker might prefer to stop selling to the U.S. government entirely rather than cut U.S. prices, which could defeat the policy instead of forcing compliance.

The requirement applies only to manufacturers that enter contracts with the United States for drug sales, so a manufacturer that avoided federal contracts would escape the price cap altogether, limiting how much relief it could actually deliver.

The price benchmark is the manufacturer's average price in just six foreign nations, set by regulation by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and the bill leaves key details — which transactions count, which are exempt — to agency discretion rather than fixing them in law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors would have been large and direct: roughly a 40 percent average cut in brand-name drug prices, at a time when Medicare covered no outpatient drugs and seniors paid full retail. The design is blunt, however. Tying compliance to federal contracting is a leaky enforcement mechanism, and the threat of debarment could push manufacturers out of federal sales rather than into lower prices. A cheaper public alternative abroad was real; the bill's main weakness was how it would force prices down, not whether the price gap existed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and then to their Health subcommittees in April 2001, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003 without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Allen of Maine introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness for Seniors Act on April 4, 2001, with a long list of Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced.
In late April 2001 it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 107th Congress.
It ended with 127 cosponsors — 126 of 208 House Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent — but no Republican cosponsor, and it never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they kept charging U.S. seniors the higher domestic prices the bill targeted, since the bill died in subcommittee without any vote ever being scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: 126 of 208 House Democrats plus the chamber's one Independent cosponsored, and no Republican did. With Republicans holding the House majority and both committee chairs, the bill never left subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers that sell to the U.S. government to supply pharmacies at their average foreign price, closing the gap between high U.S. prices and lower prices abroad — a direct hit to the pricing power that produced $27.3 billion in industry profits in 1999, per the bill's findings. The bill's defeat preserved that pricing power, including charging Medicare beneficiaries full retail with no drug benefit in place.

Pharmacies would have gained a right to buy covered drugs at the capped foreign price in quantities matching Medicare beneficiaries' purchases, with no direct requirement to pass savings on beyond serving beneficiaries. The effect is modest either way; the bill regulates manufacturers, not pharmacies.
